citation: (1) University of Copenhagen press release, English: 'Discovery of curse ritual in rubbish dump surprises Egyptologist: "It must have been widespread in ancient Egypt"', 23.11.2026 08:54 CET, via Ritzau (via.ritzau.dk/pressemeddelelse/15297191/...) and mirrored verbatim on EurekAlert (eurekalert.org/news-releases/1152895, News Release 23-Nov-2026; press contact Carsten Munk Hansen, UCPH Communications). (2) University of Copenhagen press release, Danish: 'Fund af forbandelsesritual i affaldsdynge overrasker egyptolog: "Det må have været meget udbredt i oldtidens Egypten"', 23.11.2026 07:59 CET, via Ritzau (via.ritzau.dk/pressemeddelelse/15296814/...). No standalone news.ku.dk / nyheder.ku.dk page was found; the Ritzau releases are KU's own distribution. (3) Phys.org, 'Discovery of curse ritual in trash dump surprises Egyptologist: "It must have been widespread in ancient Egypt"', 23 Nov 2026, 'Provided by University of Copenhagen', edited by Gaby Clark, reviewed by Robert Egan (phys.org/news/2026-11-discovery-curse-ritual-trash-dump.html). (4) Dario Radley, 'Charred papyrus from a Theban rubbish heap is the earliest physical evidence of the Egyptian Apophis curse ritual', Archaeology News Online Magazine (archaeologymag.com/2026/11/charred-papyrus-the-apophis-curse-ritual/), 24 Nov 2026. Paper all four report on: Fredrik Hagen, Carina Kühne-Wespi, Myriam Seco Álvarez, 'Cursing Apophis: Text and Material Culture of an Egyptian Execration Ritual', ZÄS 153(2): 214-239, doi 10.1515/zaes-2026-0004 (CC BY 4.0, per Crossref).
evidence_tier: Press release (KU English and Danish versions; EurekAlert and Phys.org reproduce the English release) and secondary press (archaeologymag.com rewrite, which also draws on the paper). None is peer-reviewed; only the ZÄS paper is.
access_status: KU English release: fully read (raw HTML from Ritzau and EurekAlert, identical text). KU Danish release: fully read (raw HTML from Ritzau). archaeologymag.com: fully read (raw HTML). Phys.org: direct download blocked by a bot check; read only through a summarising fetch tool, so its body text was confirmed sentence by sentence only for selected passages (credit line, GIST box, the 'new indication' and 'widely used outside temples' wording, use of 'trash'). Paper: abstract and metadata only (Crossref); the De Gruyter Brill full text returned empty or 405 to automated requests, so the paper body was NOT opened.
exact_quotes:
KU English release (Ritzau / EurekAlert, identical):
- Subhead: "Forty papyrus fragments found in a rubbish deposit more than 3,000 years old turned out to be the burnt remains of a curse ritual. According to Egyptologist Fredrik Hagen, signs of mass production suggest the ritual was widespread and commonly practised in ancient Egypt."
- Body: "The fragments show that the ritual was probably far more widespread and commonplace than previously believed."
- Body: "Until recently, Egyptologists only had a single copy of the so-called “Apophis-ritual”, preserved in a ritual manual from the late fourth century BC, but with little independent evidence for how often it was performed, by whom, or where."
- Body: "Professor of Egyptology Fredrik Hagen from the University of Copenhagen and his colleagues discovered 40 charred and pierced papyrus fragments in a rubbish deposit. The fragments turned out to be mass-produced copies of drawings and texts that were burnt during the Apophis ritual."
- Hagen: "These tiny fragments give us a new indication of how widespread curse rituals were in ancient Egypt. Our finds and the subsequent analysis of the ritual confirms that it was a regular part of temple life, but a quick look at references to the ritual in other contexts also show that it was widely used outside temples, and that it was a common feature of Egyptian culture more broadly."
- Hagen: "We know that literate people, including those who were not priests, had access to magical rituals and functioned as magicians and healers. It is clear that people approached scribes for help in performing magic, both for protection and for attacking others. That includes the curse rituals that we can now see were far more widespread than previously thought."
- Body: "The fragments excavated by Fredrik Hagen and his colleagues are around 3,400 years old, pushing back the dating of the ritual by 1,000 years."
- Hagen: "They show that the ritual was much older than the one surviving copy from the fourth century BC might suggest. Already 1,000 years earlier, during what we call the New Kingdom, it was an integrated part of Egyptian culture, and our article also looks at the types of priests who were responsible for carrying out the ritual in the temples"
- Body: "The fragments, each no larger than half a postage stamp, also constitute the earliest physical evidence that the curse ritual was carried out in practice."
- Hagen: "The papyrus drawing was often completely destroyed during the ritual, when it was trampled on, spit on, pierced with a knife and ultimately burned. Many of the 40 fragments show signs of having been pierced and charred, which matches the ritual instructions remarkably well. For the ritual to be successful, the materials had to be destroyed by fire, so we are extremely fortunate to have found any of them in a condition that still allows them to be recognised and studied,"
- Hagen: "The reason physical remains of this ritual have never been found before is probably also that few people have paid much attention to such rather unglamorous rubbish dumps,"
- Hagen: "The fragments from the curse ritual, even if they are remarkable, are just a small piece of the puzzle. Other papyrus fragments from the same area have turned out to be the remains of the administrative archive of the temple, which enables us to investigate the daily economy and logistics of the offering cult in a temple like this."
- Box 'About the Apophis ritual': "In Egyptian mythology, Apophis was the serpent of chaos that attempted each night to prevent the sun god Ra from completing his journey through the underworld." / "To protect the order of the world, ancient Egyptians, typically priests, performed rituals intended to symbolically destroy Apophis and his powers." / "As part of the ritual, Apophis was drawn in the shape of a snake and his name written on papyrus in red ink, or represented as a wax figure. The papyrus or figures were then pierced with knives and burned while magical spells were recited." / "The new archaeological discoveries from the mortuary temple of Thutmose III in Thebes show that the ritual was already being practised during the New Kingdom more than 3,400 years ago."
- Photo caption: "An almost completely preserved example of an Apophis papyrus, showing a drawing in red ink of the serpent-form of Apophis with three knives cutting into his body, with his name in the hieratic at the top."

KU Danish release (Ritzau), with English gloss:
- Headline quote: "Det må have været meget udbredt i oldtidens Egypten" (It must have been very widespread in ancient Egypt).
- "Indtil for nylig har egyptologerne kun haft et enkelt 2.400 år gammelt eksemplar af det såkaldte ”Apophis-ritual”" (Until recently Egyptologists had only a single 2,400-year-old copy of the so-called Apophis ritual).
- Hagen: "De her bittesmå fragmenter giver os en helt ny forståelse af, hvor udbredte forbandelsesritualer har været i oldtidens Egypten. Vores analyse viser, at de ikke kun har været forbeholdt konger og præster, men også været en del af almindelige menneskers liv og var en udbredt og fast del af egyptisk kultur" (These tiny fragments give us an entirely new understanding of how widespread curse rituals were in ancient Egypt. Our analysis shows that they were not reserved for kings and priests but were also part of ordinary people's lives and a widespread, fixed part of Egyptian culture).
- Hagen: "Det er veldokumenteret, at alle skriftkyndige - også dem, der ikke var præster - havde adgang til magiske ritualer. Derfor er det en rimelig antagelse, at folk har kontaktet skriftkyndige for at få hjælp til at udføre magi." (It is well documented that all literate people, including non-priests, had access to magical rituals. It is therefore a reasonable assumption that people contacted literate people for help performing magic.)
- Hagen: "De bekræfter, at ritualet er blevet udført i over 1.000 år på præcis den måde, som instruktionerne i den 2.400 år gamle tekst beskriver." (They confirm that the ritual was performed for over 1,000 years in precisely the way the instructions in the 2,400-year-old text describe.)
- Hagen: "De 40 fragmenter er netop gennemhullede og forkullede, hvilket viser, at de har været brugt i praksis som del af ritualet" (The 40 fragments are indeed perforated and charred, which shows they were used in practice as part of the ritual).
- Hagen: "Grunden til, at der aldrig er fundet sådan nogle fysiske rester af ritualet tidligere, er formentlig, at man ikke tidligere har interesseret sig for sådan nogle kedelige affaldsdynger" (The reason no such physical remains have been found before is probably that no one has previously been interested in such boring rubbish heaps).
- Box: "viser, at ritualet blev udført i praksis allerede i det Nye Rige for mere end 3.000 år siden" (shows the ritual was performed in practice already in the New Kingdom more than 3,000 years ago).

Phys.org (via summarising fetch; partial): credit "Provided by University of Copenhagen"; note "This article has been reviewed according to Science X's editorial process and policies." LLM-generated GIST box: "Forty charred papyrus fragments from a temple trash deposit in Thebes provide the earliest physical evidence of the Apophis curse ritual, dating back about 3,400 years. Piercing and burning match ritual instructions, indicating routine temple use roughly 1,000 years before the previously known manual." Labelled as "automatically generated using LLM". Body uses "trash deposit" and "trash dumps" where KU says "rubbish".

archaeologymag.com (Radley, 24 Nov 2026):
- "They are the earliest direct physical evidence of the ritual, and they suggest it was far more widespread and commonplace than scholars believed."
- "The study also presents a later, very similar piece (P. MMA 28.3.113) and compares the fragments with the text of the manual."
- "Mass production points to regular demand. Hagen says the finds confirm the ritual was part of temple life, and references in other contexts show wide use outside temples too."
- "A decree for Amenhotep son of Hapu, a long hieratic stela probably from his memorial temple at Thebes, warns those who might take resources and personnel from the institution that the king's uraeus will spit fire on their foreheads, blacken their flesh, and eat their limbs, so they become like Apophis on the morning of the New Year Festival."
- "The authors say how well known it was is hard to judge, but suggest it was probably not far behind the Opening of the Mouth Ritual, the Daily Temple Ritual, and the Daily Cult Ritual."
- Caption on P. MMA 28.3.113: "The serpent figure, with its head turned downwards, is cut by a single knife across the body. The squares would have been cut along the dividing lines before use."

Paper abstract (Crossref, verbatim): "Excavations at the mortuary temple of Thutmose III have revealed papyrus fragments that were produced for, and then burnt during, the ritual known as 'Overthrowing Apophis', through which the arch-enemy of the sun god Re was cursed. The article presents some of these New Kingdom fragments as well as a later but very similar piece (P. MMA 28.3.113), and compares them with the text of the ritual instructions from a 3rd Century BC papyrus (P. Bremner-Rhind = BM EA 10188). The use and social context of the ritual is also discussed."
date_and_recency: KU releases 23 Nov 2026 (Danish 07:59 CET, English 08:54 CET); EurekAlert 23 Nov 2026; Phys.org 23 Nov 2026; archaeologymag.com 24 Nov 2026 13:45 UTC. Paper: Crossref published date 3 Nov 2026; EurekAlert lists 'Article Publication Date 5-Nov-2026'. Material discussed: New Kingdom fragments from the mortuary temple of Thutmose III, described as 'around 3,400 years old', compared with P. Bremner-Rhind (release: 'late fourth century BC'; abstract: '3rd Century BC').
key_claims: 1. Forty charred and pierced papyrus fragments were found in a rubbish deposit at a temple in Thebes (the mortuary temple of Thutmose III). 2. They are 'mass-produced copies of drawings and texts that were burnt during the Apophis ritual'. 3. They are 'the earliest physical evidence that the curse ritual was carried out in practice'. 4. They push the dating of the ritual back by 1,000 years, into the New Kingdom; Hagen: 'Already 1,000 years earlier... it was an integrated part of Egyptian culture'. 5. Before this, Egyptologists had 'only a single copy' of the ritual, in a late-fourth-century BC manual, with little evidence of how often, by whom or where it was performed. 6. Piercing and charring on the fragments 'matches the ritual instructions remarkably well'. 7. The ritual was 'a regular part of temple life' and, from 'a quick look at references to the ritual in other contexts', 'widely used outside temples' and 'a common feature of Egyptian culture more broadly'. 8. Literate non-priests acted as magicians and healers, and people approached scribes for magic 'both for protection and for attacking others'. 9. Remains were not found before probably because few looked at 'unglamorous rubbish dumps'. 10. The paper also discusses which types of priests performed the ritual. 11. The ritual began as a curse on Ra's serpent enemy and was adapted to curse the pharaoh's enemies or anyone, poison and bad weather, to treat illness and to secure personal success. Danish version adds: curse rituals were 'not reserved for kings and priests but also part of ordinary people's lives', and the ritual was performed 'for over 1,000 years in precisely the way' the manual describes. archaeologymag adds, apparently from the paper: P. MMA 28.3.113 as a later comparandum, the Amenhotep son of Hapu decree as a curse referring to Apophis on New Year's morning, and the authors' view that the ritual was probably not far behind the Opening of the Mouth, Daily Temple and Daily Cult rituals in how well known it was.
headline_figures:
- '40' / 'Forty' papyrus fragments ('40 charred and pierced papyrus fragments'; 'Many of the 40 fragments show signs of having been pierced and charred'). Basis: release. The abstract says only that the article 'presents some of these New Kingdom fragments'; no count in the abstract.
- 'around 3,400 years old' (fragments); 'more than 3,400 years ago' (English box); 'more than 3,000 years old' (English subhead) and 'mere end 3.000 år siden' (Danish box). Basis: release; no dating method stated.
- 'pushing back the dating of the ritual by 1,000 years'; 'Already 1,000 years earlier'. Basis: release, relative to the Bremner-Rhind manual.
- Manual date: 'late fourth century BC' (English release), '2.400 år gammelt' / 2,400 years old (Danish release), '3rd Century BC' (paper abstract).
- Size: 'each no larger than half a postage stamp'.
- 'a single copy' of the ritual (manual) before this find.
- Paper: ZÄS vol. 153, issue 2, pp. 214-239; three authors (Crossref).
dating_and_context: Findspot: 'a rubbish deposit' / 'rubbish dumps outside the temple' at 'the mortuary temple of Thutmose III in Thebes' (release); archaeologymag: 'a Theban rubbish heap'. Date: 'around 3,400 years old', 'during what we call the New Kingdom'. The release gives no dating method (no mention of pottery, stratigraphy or palaeography) and no reign or dynasty beyond the temple's owner. 3,400 years before present is about 1375 BC, which is close to but slightly after the reign of Thutmose III (c. 1479-1425 BC); whether the dump material dates to his reign or later use of the temple is not stated in the press [uncertain]. Other fragments from the same area are the temple's administrative archive.
what_it_says_about_apophis: Release: 'the great snake who was the main enemy of the sungod Ra'; the ritual 'would help the sun on its journey through the underworld during the night, when he had to fight off the serpent in order to reemerge in the morning'. Box: 'Apophis was the serpent of chaos that attempted each night to prevent the sun god Ra from completing his journey through the underworld'; priests performed rituals 'to protect the order of the world' and 'symbolically destroy Apophis and his powers'. Danish: 'solgudens ærkefjende og hans allierede' (the sun god's arch-enemy and his allies). Abstract: 'the arch-enemy of the sun god Re'. The nightly framing implies repeated, never-final combat, but none of the press says outright whether Apophis is ever finally defeated. archaeologymag cites the decree's 'like Apophis on the morning of the New Year Festival', tying the ritual to the start of the year.
ritual_practice: Release box: Apophis 'drawn in the shape of a snake and his name written on papyrus in red ink, or represented as a wax figure', then 'pierced with knives and burned while magical spells were recited'. Hagen: the drawing was 'trampled on, spit on, pierced with a knife and ultimately burned'. Fragments are 'mass-produced copies of drawings and texts'; the caption shows a near-complete example 'with three knives cutting into his body, with his name in the hieratic at the top'. archaeologymag: the MMA sheet has 'squares of drawings' that 'would have been cut along the dividing lines before use'. Performers: 'typically priests'; the paper 'looks at the types of priests who were responsible for carrying out the ritual in the temples'; Hagen also says literate non-priests acted as magicians and people went to scribes for help. Place: in temples (Thutmose III mortuary temple) and, per Hagen, 'widely used outside temples'. Danish box omits the drawing and red ink, saying only that the name was written on papyrus or the snake made as wax figures.
prescribed_vs_attested_frequency: The press gives no prescribed frequency (no daily or hourly schedule from Bremner-Rhind) and no count of performances. Frequency is inferred qualitatively: 'mass-produced', 'a regular part of temple life', 'widespread and commonly practised'. The English release itself admits the earlier state of knowledge had 'little independent evidence for how often it was performed'. The jump from 40 small fragments in one temple dump to 'widespread' and 'common feature of Egyptian culture more broadly' rests, by Hagen's own words, partly on 'a quick look at references to the ritual in other contexts'. Any minimum-number-of-performances figure must come from the paper, which was not opened [uncertain].
relevance_to_angle: Supports: mass-produced sheets cut from grids, burnt and dumped, read as consumables of a routine, repeated temple job rather than a one-off rite; the nightly-attack framing fits chaos held off by maintenance; Hagen's emphasis on 'unglamorous rubbish dumps' and the temple's 'daily economy and logistics' is itself a maintenance-over-monuments argument. Complicates: the press stresses widespread and private use (curses on personal enemies, illness, weather, personal success), which shifts the ritual from cosmic maintenance toward everyday magic and personal attack; 'regular' is not quantified; and the strongest frequency wording is press-release interpretation, not demonstrated counts.
limitations_stated: English release: before the find there was 'little independent evidence for how often it was performed, by whom, or where'; 'we are extremely fortunate to have found any of them' because 'the materials had to be destroyed by fire'; the fragments 'are just a small piece of the puzzle'; the outside-temple claim rests on 'a quick look at references to the ritual in other contexts'. Danish release hedges the scribes claim as 'en rimelig antagelse' (a reasonable assumption) and the papyrus destruction as 'formentlig' (probably). archaeologymag, reporting the paper: 'how well known it was is hard to judge'. Abstract: the article 'presents some of these New Kingdom fragments'.
source_discrepancies:
1. Headline quote 'It must have been widespread in ancient Egypt' (Danish 'Det må have været meget udbredt') appears only in the headline; no body quote from Hagen uses those words. It is a headline paraphrase presented in quotation marks.
2. English vs Danish Hagen quotes differ in substance: English 'a new indication' vs Danish 'en helt ny forståelse' (an entirely new understanding); Danish 'not reserved for kings and priests but also part of ordinary people's lives' has no English counterpart; English 'It is clear that people approached scribes' vs Danish 'it is a reasonable assumption'; English 'Many of the 40 fragments show signs of having been pierced and charred' vs Danish 'De 40 fragmenter er netop gennemhullede og forkullede' (the 40 fragments are perforated and charred), implying all 40; Danish 'performed for over 1,000 years in precisely the way' the manual describes vs English 'matches the ritual instructions remarkably well'.
3. Bremner-Rhind date: English release 'late fourth century BC', Danish '2,400 years old', paper abstract '3rd Century BC'.
4. Age: 'around 3,400 years old' / 'more than 3,400 years ago' vs 'more than 3,000 years' (English subhead, Danish box).
5. Fragment count: press '40'; abstract 'some of these' fragments; outline caveat notes a possible 12+14+16=42 total in the paper (not checked here).
6. Paper publication date: Crossref 3 Nov 2026; EurekAlert 5 Nov 2026.
7. Phys.org changes 'rubbish' to 'trash' and adds an LLM-generated GIST claiming 'routine temple use', wording not in the release.
8. 'Pushing back the dating of the ritual by 1,000 years' conflates the first physical evidence with the ritual's age; the release's own claim is about physical remains, and the paper (per archaeologymag) cites a New Kingdom decree alluding to the curse, so textual allusions predating Bremner-Rhind were already known [uncertain].
9. archaeologymag includes paper content absent from the release (P. MMA 28.3.113, Amenhotep son of Hapu decree, comparison with Opening of the Mouth etc.), which matches the abstract's mention of P. MMA 28.3.113.

Wording that likely goes beyond the paper (judged against the abstract only, since the full text was not opened) [uncertain]: 'It must have been widespread' (headline); 'widely used outside temples' and 'a common feature of Egyptian culture more broadly'; 'far more widespread than previously thought'; Danish 'part of ordinary people's lives' and 'performed for over 1,000 years in precisely the way'; Phys.org GIST 'routine temple use'; 'pushing back the dating of the ritual by 1,000 years'. The abstract claims only that fragments were 'produced for, and then burnt during' the ritual and that 'the use and social context of the ritual is also discussed'.
verification_status: Checked against opened sources: all KU English quotes (Ritzau and EurekAlert raw text, identical); all KU Danish quotes (Ritzau raw text); all archaeologymag quotes (raw text); paper title, authors, volume, pages, licence and abstract (Crossref). Partly checked: Phys.org body (summarising tool only; credit line, GIST, 'trash' wording and two key phrases confirmed, full verbatim body not seen) [uncertain]. Not checked against the paper body: the count of 40, the 3,400-year date and its method, 'mass-produced', 'widely used outside temples', the priests discussion, the decree for Amenhotep son of Hapu, the Bremner-Rhind date the authors use in the body, and any minimum number of performances [uncertain]. No ku.dk news page was found; the Ritzau releases are treated as the KU original.
